title: Solutions and colligative properties
note: Molarity (mol solute per liter of solution) is the everyday concentration unit; molality (mol solute per kg of solvent) is used for colligative properties because it does not change with temperature. Colligative properties depend only on how many solute particles are present: ΔTf = i·Kf·m, ΔTb = i·Kb·m, Π = iMRT. An ionic solute counts every ion it releases.

read.title: Counting particles, not identities
text: A solution is a uniform mixture of a solute dissolved in a solvent. Whether something dissolves depends on matching attractions. Polar water dissolves salt and sugar well, while nonpolar oil does not mix with it. Gases behave differently: they dissolve better at higher pressure, as Henry's law says, and worse in warm water, which is why a warm soda goes flat quickly.

Some properties of a solution depend on what is dissolved, such as color or taste. Others, called colligative properties, depend only on how many solute particles are present. Adding a nonvolatile solute lowers the solvent's vapor pressure, raises its boiling point, lowers its freezing point, and creates osmotic pressure across a membrane that lets only solvent through.

For freezing and boiling points, the size of the change is the solvent's constant times the molality of particles. Water's freezing point constant is 1.86 °C/m, so a 1.00 m sugar solution freezes near −1.86 °C. Ionic compounds break into ions, so they count more than once. One formula unit of NaCl gives two particles and CaCl₂ gives three, which is why calcium chloride lowers the freezing point of road slush more than the same molality of table salt. In real solutions, ions attract each other, so the effective number of particles is a bit lower than the ideal count.

q.q: What determines the size of a colligative effect?
o: The molar mass of the solvent only

q.q: Why does CaCl₂ lower the freezing point more than NaCl at the same molality?
o: It releases three ions per formula unit instead of two

q.q: Why does a warm soda go flat faster than a cold one?
o: Gases are less soluble in warmer liquids
